Debilitate

/dih-BIL-i-tayt/ — rhymes with activate · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To debilitate someone or something is to make it very weak, often so it can no longer function normally.

The heat wave debilitated the marathoners long before the finish.

Worked Example

A long illness debilitated the elderly patient until she could no longer walk to the mailbox.

Debilitate is precise because it specifically means to weaken someone to the point of losing normal function, not merely to tire or inconvenience them.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

weaken: To weaken something is simply to reduce its strength, by any amount — a cold can weaken you for a day. To debilitate goes much further: it drains strength so thoroughly that normal life stops working, the difference between feeling weaker and being unable to function.

exhaust: To exhaust someone is to use up their energy completely — after the race she was exhausted, but a night's sleep restored her. To debilitate is not about spent energy; it is lasting damage to strength itself, weakness that rest alone does not repair.

impair: To impair something is to damage how well it works — an injury can impair your hearing without touching your strength. To debilitate attacks strength itself, draining the body until it can barely function. Impair says the machinery is faulty; debilitate says the power is gone.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

invigorate: fill with fresh energy and strength

strengthen: make stronger or more powerful

Where it sits · how thoroughly strength is drained — weariness → weakness → helplessness → debilitate

weariness vs. debilitate: Weariness is far milder than debilitation; weariness is ordinary tiredness, while to debilitate is to weaken someone so badly they can barely function.

weakness vs. debilitate: Plain weakness is milder than debilitation; weakness is a simple lack of strength, while to debilitate drains that strength until normal activity becomes impossible.

helplessness vs. debilitate: Helplessness is close to debilitation, but to debilitate names the process of being weakened, while helplessness is the extreme state of being unable to act at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: away from, opposite of (Latin)

Root — bilit

Root — bilit: strength (from Latin debilis, 'weak' — literally strength taken away; PIE bel-, 'strong')

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make, to do (verb-forming) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: De- ('away from') + bilit ('strength,' from Latin debilis, 'weak' — literally strength taken away) + -ate ('to make'): to debilitate is to take strength away — to make someone or something very weak.

Use the root in a new word: debility

Use the root in a new word: debility: A long illness can leave a person in a state of debility, or weakness — the same root that lets a disease debilitate the body.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / neutral

Debilitate is a forceful word for serious, lasting weakness that prevents normal function. Use it when describing how an illness, injury, or hardship weakens someone to dysfunction. For milder tiredness or temporary fatigue, 'tired' or 'weak' is simpler and more precise.
